title: Esther 4:12–17
context: Mordecai answers Esther’s hesitation with a sharp warning: she will not escape in the king’s house more than the other Jews (4:12–13). If she stays silent, relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place, but she and her father’s house will perish; and who knows whether she has come to the kingdom for such a time as this (4:14)? Esther then asks Mordecai to gather the Jews in Susa to fast for her three days, night and day, while she and her maidens fast too, and she resolves to go to the king against the law: if she perishes, she perishes (4:15–16). Mordecai does as she commands (4:17). The book does not name God, even in 4:14. Many readers in both traditions hear “another place” and “for such a time as this” as pointing to God’s providence, while others take “another place” more narrowly as some other human source of help; this commentary notes the range and does not overread the silence. Reading 4:14 providentially is shared ground for Arminian and Reformed readers rather than a point of division. On how fasting and prayer relate to God’s purposes, compare the discussion at Joshua 10:14. Some readers suggest that a fast begun soon after the decree of the thirteenth day of the first month (3:12) would have overlapped Passover; the text does not say so.

verses.text: They told Esther’s words to Mordecai.
verses.arminianNotes: Esther’s words are carried to Mordecai. Arminian readers note that the go-betweens keep the dialogue moving and that Mordecai receives her real hesitation rather than a polished refusal. The narrative respects Esther’s fear as a real feature of the decision she must make.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the exchange as a test in which Esther’s understandable caution will be met by a word that reframes her position. They see the conversation as the ordinary means through which God brings her to resolve. Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse as the turning point of the dialogue and avoid treating Esther’s hesitation as faithlessness.

verses.text: Then Mordecai asked them to return this answer to Esther: “Don’t think to yourself that you will escape in the king’s house any more than all the Jews.
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai warns Esther not to think she will escape in the king’s house any more than the other Jews. Arminian readers see Mordecai confronting her with the truth that her privileged position cannot shield her from the fate of her people, and they stress that the warning appeals to her responsibility and solidarity, inviting a free response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the warning as stripping away false security, and they note that it calls Esther to identify with the covenant people whose destiny she shares. Shared ground: both traditions read Mordecai’s words as bracing but loving, and both see the verse as a summons to costly faithfulness rather than self-protection, without needing to settle Esther’s inner state.

verses.text: For if you remain silent now, then relief and deliverance will come to the Jews from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish. Who knows if you haven’t come to the kingdom for such a time as this?”
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai is confident that relief and deliverance will come from another place if Esther is silent, yet he asks whether she has come to the kingdom for such a time as this. God is not named. Arminian readers often hear a faithful providence that will preserve the people, along with a real invitation to Esther, whose response truly matters for her own house and for how deliverance comes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often hear the same providence, seeing God as having placed Esther in the palace as the appointed means for this moment, while her choice remains real and accountable. Shared ground: both traditions affirm that God’s care for his people does not depend on one person yet calls that person to act, note that some readers take “another place” as human help, and treat this verse as shared ground, not a contrast.

verses.text: Then Esther asked them to answer Mordecai,
verses.arminianNotes: Esther sends her answer back to Mordecai. Arminian readers see this as the moment Esther moves from hesitation to resolve, a real change in her own heart prompted by Mordecai’s words. Her answer will show courage freely embraced rather than forced upon her.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a decisive turn and read it as God at work through Mordecai’s word to strengthen Esther for her task. They note that her response begins with a call for communal support. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the hinge between Mordecai’s challenge and Esther’s commitment, and both see her resolve as genuinely hers.

verses.text: “Go, gather together all the Jews who are present in Susa, and fast for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day. I and my maidens will also fast the same way. Then I will go in to the king, which is against the law; and if I perish, I perish.”
verses.arminianNotes: Esther asks the Jews of Susa to fast for her three days, and she and her maidens will fast too; then she will go to the king, against the law, and if she perishes, she perishes. Arminian readers see costly, freely chosen courage, and many assume the fast was joined to prayer, though the text does not say so. Her resolve shows trust that does not presume on the outcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise admire Esther’s self-surrender and read the communal fast as dependence on God, implied rather than stated, the ordinary means through which God brings about his purposes. Shared ground: both traditions read “if I perish, I perish” as courage, not fatalism, note that prayer is inferred rather than mentioned, and point to the discussion at Joshua 10:14 on how prayer and God’s purposes relate.

verses.text: So Mordecai went his way, and did according to all that Esther had commanded him.
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai goes and does all that Esther commanded. Arminian readers note the reversal in which Mordecai, who had instructed Esther (2:10, 2:20, 4:8), now follows her direction. Her leadership is real and freely exercised, and the community’s response is part of how the story moves toward deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the shift in roles and see God raising Esther to lead at the decisive moment, with Mordecai and the community supporting her through the fast. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing a united community gathered behind Esther and see the change in authority between Mordecai and Esther as a deliberate narrative turn.
